posts.excerpt: ErrorCopy: AI Error Explainer turns a VS Code diagnostic and its surrounding code into a structured prompt, then sends it to GitHub Copilot, or opens Copilot Web, Claude, or ChatGPT with the prompt ready to paste.
posts.body:
Most error messages are only half the story. A TypeScript message such as "Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'" tells you that two types disagree, but not which value caused it, which call produced it, or what the code around it is doing. To get a useful answer from an AI assistant, developers usually reconstruct that missing context by hand: they copy the message, find the line, scroll up to the function, and paste it all into a chat window. It works, but it's slow, and the result depends on how much context the developer remembered to include.

ErrorCopy: AI Error Explainer is a VS Code extension that automates that step. It reads the diagnostic directly from the editor, gathers the code around it, and builds a consistent prompt that you can send to the AI tool of your choice. This post explains what the extension captures, why it routes requests the way it does, how it handles privacy, and what its current limitations are.

## What the extension captures

ErrorCopy reads the diagnostic from VS Code's language diagnostics API, not from text on the screen. That matters because the editor already holds structured information about each problem, and copying the visible text would throw most of it away. For the diagnostic under the cursor, the extension collects:

- The diagnostic message, its severity, and its source, such as TypeScript or ESLint
- The diagnostic code, when the language server provides one
- The exact range of the problem, rather than only the line number
- Related information that the language server attaches to the diagnostic
- Any text the developer has selected, so the prompt can point at the exact expression
- The surrounding code, limited to a configurable number of lines
- The language identifier and the line number

All of this is assembled into a Markdown prompt with fixed sections. Because the structure is the same for every error, the prompt reads the same whether it came from a compiler, a linter, or a language server, and the AI tool receives the same kind of input each time.

## Two commands, one prompt

The extension has two entry points. Copy Error with Context, bound to Ctrl+Shift+E on Windows and Linux and Cmd+Shift+E on macOS, builds the prompt and places it on the clipboard. It doesn't send anything anywhere. Explain This Error does the same work, then opens a picker so you can choose a destination. Both use the same prompt builder, so the output is identical either way.

## Why there are two kinds of destination

The providers fall into two groups, and the difference between them drives most of the design.

GitHub Copilot is handled through VS Code's Language Model API. The extension selects an available Copilot model, sends the prompt, and streams the response into a dedicated output channel called ErrorCopy Copilot. This keeps the answer inside the editor. It requires an active Copilot subscription, a signed-in VS Code account, and the user's permission for the extension to use the model. If no model is available, ErrorCopy keeps the prompt on the clipboard and tells the user what to do next, so the request isn't lost.

Copilot Web, Claude, and ChatGPT work differently. These sites don't offer an API that an extension can use to submit a prompt, and their chat inputs are controlled by the page itself. An extension can't reliably fill those fields, and any attempt to do so would break whenever the site changed its markup. So ErrorCopy copies the prompt, opens the site, and leaves the final paste to the user. It's one extra keystroke, but it's predictable, and it works with any account the user already has.

Stack Overflow is a third case. It isn't an AI provider. ErrorCopy builds a search from the diagnostic text and opens the results, because a large share of common errors already have accepted answers. Including it gives users a non-AI path when they want one.

The trade-off is clear. Copilot gives the most integrated experience, but only for users who have access to it. The browser providers work for everyone, but they require a manual step. Supporting both means the extension doesn't depend on a single vendor, and a new provider can be added to the same prompt pipeline without changing how diagnostics are collected.

## Privacy and data handling

ErrorCopy has no backend. It doesn't store the user's code, it doesn't collect telemetry, and it doesn't call any AI service on its own behalf. The only time a prompt leaves the machine is when the user chooses a destination. If the user picks Copilot, the prompt goes to a model through VS Code's Language Model API. If the user picks a browser provider, nothing is sent until they paste the prompt into that site.

Before a prompt is built, the extension masks common secret patterns, including API keys, tokens, passwords, and Bearer credentials. Pattern-based masking is a safety net, not a guarantee. It can't recognise every secret format, so users should still read the prompt before sending it, especially when working in a codebase that holds real credentials.

File paths are excluded by default. A path can reveal a username, a company name, or the layout of a private repository, and none of that is needed to explain most errors. Users who want paths included can enable them in settings. The same setting governs any file locations that appear in related diagnostics, so the default applies consistently.

## Configuration

Three settings control how much of the editor's content is shared:

- errorCopy.includeFilePath, which is off by default, adds the file path to the prompt.
- errorCopy.includeSurroundingCode, which is on by default, includes the code around the error.
- errorCopy.maxContextLines, which defaults to 12 and can be set from 2 to 40, limits how many lines of surrounding code are included.

Together these let a developer decide how much code leaves the editor, from only the diagnostic message to a wider window of the file.

## Engineering decisions

The extension is written in TypeScript against the VS Code API. Type checking catches mistakes in calls to the editor and the diagnostics API before the code runs, which matters because many of those mistakes would otherwise only show up inside the Extension Development Host.

The build uses esbuild to bundle the entry point, src/extension.ts, into a single CommonJS file, out/extension.js, targeting Node 20. The vscode module is marked as external, because VS Code supplies it at runtime and must not be bundled. A single output file keeps activation fast and keeps the package small.

Packaging is controlled by .vscodeignore. Source files, configuration, and tests are excluded, so the published package contains only the compiled bundle, the manifest, the README, the changelog, and the license. Before publishing, I confirmed the package contents by listing them, rather than assuming the ignore rules were correct.

One issue appeared only when the project was cloned onto a different machine. The build script referenced a Windows-specific path to the esbuild binary, so compilation failed elsewhere. I replaced that with a command that npm resolves on every platform. It's a small change, but it's the kind of problem that only shows up when someone other than the original author builds the project.

## Current limitations

The extension has no automated tests that run inside the VS Code Extension Host yet. Validation so far combines type checking, a production build, packaging checks, and manual testing of the packaged extension. That's adequate for a first release, but it isn't a substitute for tests that exercise commands and diagnostics inside the editor, and adding them is the next priority.

Other limits are inherent to the design. The browser providers require a manual paste. Copilot access depends on the user's subscription and sign-in state. Secret masking is heuristic. And Ctrl+Shift+E captures only diagnostics the language server has reported, so an error printed in the terminal or raised at runtime is outside its scope.

## What's next

The priorities for the next release are automated Extension Host tests, covering command registration, prompt content, clipboard fallback, and the Copilot path when no model is available. After that, the same prompt pipeline could support additional providers, and I'd like to refine the prompt structure based on the errors people actually send through it.

## Try it and tell me what's missing

ErrorCopy: AI Error Explainer can be installed from the Extensions view in VS Code by searching for its name. The source code and issue tracker are on GitHub at github.com/gidadomukhtar/error-copy-pro.

If you try it, the most useful feedback is a specific case where the prompt didn't include the context you needed. Those cases show exactly where the prompt builder should improve.

Adding Field Keyword Patterns to the .NET Docs
posts.excerpt: My pull request to Microsoft's official .NET documentation adds practical examples of the C# 14 field keyword. It was reviewed and merged by the .NET docs team.
posts.body:
C# 14 adds the field keyword, which lets a property use its own compiler-generated backing field. The existing docs explained the syntax, but readers had no practical patterns to copy.

My pull request adds a section called Common patterns with field, with three examples:

- Lazy initialization, where a getter creates the value the first time it is read.
- MVVM property notifications, where a setter raises a change event only when the value actually changes.
- Data normalization, where a setter trims and lowercases input before storing it.

Review pushed me to make the examples null-safe, use ToLowerInvariant instead of ToLower, and fix the Markdown formatting. The change was merged into the official C# 14 what's new page.

posts.title: .NET Weekly #01: AI Agents, Cross-Platform Apps and Safer NuGet Releases
posts.excerpt: This week: how AI coding agents are changing cross-platform development, and how NuGet staged publishing gives developers more control over package releases
posts.body:
.NET Weekly #01: AI Agents, Cross-Platform Apps and Safer NuGet Releases

Welcome to the first edition of .NET Weekly!

There has been quite a bit happening around the .NET ecosystem lately. Some updates are worth knowing about because they introduce new capabilities, while others are interesting because they make us reconsider how we approach problems we've been solving for years.

Two developments stood out to me this week.

The first is an experiment showing how AI coding agents could influence the way we build cross-platform applications. The second is a new NuGet feature that gives package maintainers more control over when their packages become publicly available.

Both are worth looking at, so let's get into them.

AI Is Making the Cross-Platform Conversation More Interesting

One of the things I like about the .NET ecosystem is that you don't always have to start from scratch when moving between platforms. With .NET MAUI, for example, developers can build applications for Android, iOS, macOS and Windows while sharing a significant amount of their C# code.

That approach has obvious advantages. You can maintain one application project, reuse business logic and avoid building completely separate applications for every platform.

But what if sharing the entire user interface isn't always the best option?

That is the question behind a recent experiment published on the official .NET Blog by David Ortinau.

The project, called Barista Notes, is a .NET MAUI application with around 31,000 lines of handwritten C# and more than 20 NuGet dependencies. The experiment explored whether AI coding agents could help rebuild its mobile interfaces using native platform technologies without throwing away the shared .NET logic.

The result was interesting.

Instead of using the same UI approach for Android and iOS, the experiment used Android Views for Android and UIKit for iOS. The underlying application logic remained in a shared .NET library.

The original MAUI implementation was also retained as a reference, with macOS and Windows continuing to use it.

What did the experiment actually show?

The biggest change was in the amount of shared code.

Initially, approximately 99.2% of the Android and iOS implementations was shared. After the native UI implementations were introduced, that figure dropped to 40.4%.

At first, that might sound like a disadvantage. After all, one of the main attractions of cross-platform development is writing code once and using it across multiple platforms.

But looking at the Core library gives a better picture. It still accounted for 56.4% of the Android implementation and 58.7% of the iOS implementation.

So the experiment wasn't about abandoning code reuse. It was about keeping the parts that made sense to share while allowing each platform to have its own interface.

There were also some notable performance results.

The reported median startup times were:

- Android: 1,233 ms with MAUI and 615 ms with the native implementation.
- iOS: 569 ms with MAUI and 367 ms with the native implementation.

That represents a 50% lower startup median on Android and a 35% lower startup median on iOS in this particular experiment.

Those numbers are worth paying attention to, but I wouldn't use them to conclude that native interfaces will always outperform MAUI. This was one application, tested under particular conditions. Different applications, devices and implementation choices can produce different results.

The part I found more interesting

Performance isn't the whole story.

Building a separate interface for each platform also means having more code to work with. That can introduce additional maintenance work, and the experiment didn't hide that trade-off.

When the author asked AI agents to implement a new feature in both approaches, the platform-specific implementation took approximately 1.4 times the model time of the MAUI implementation. It also generated more defect and technical feedback items.

This is an important detail because it's easy to focus on what AI can generate and forget what happens after the code has been generated.

A working screen is not necessarily a well-maintained screen. Someone still has to understand the code, test it on real devices, handle platform differences and fix issues when they appear.

AI can make the initial implementation easier, particularly when working with technologies a developer isn't very familiar with. It doesn't automatically make the long-term maintenance problem disappear.

Should .NET developers reconsider MAUI?

I don't think the takeaway is that developers should stop using .NET MAUI.

A shared UI is still a sensible choice for many applications. If your requirements are straightforward and you want to maintain a consistent experience across platforms, MAUI can save a lot of time.

What I find interesting is that AI agents are making other approaches more accessible.

Previously, a small team might have avoided separate native interfaces because of the additional development effort. Now, AI can help with some of that work, making it easier to explore alternatives.

That doesn't mean every project should have multiple UI implementations. It simply means developers have another option to evaluate when performance, platform integration or user experience demands it.

The real question should be: what does this particular application need, and what architecture can the team realistically maintain?

NuGet Staged Publishing: A Useful Addition for Package Maintainers

Let's move from application development to something that affects developers who distribute libraries and tools through NuGet.

On November 17, the .NET Blog announced staged publishing on NuGet.org.

If you've ever maintained a NuGet package, you'll understand why this is useful.

Publishing a package is an important step. Once it becomes publicly available, other developers can discover it, install it and depend on it. That makes mistakes during release particularly inconvenient.

Imagine preparing a release that contains several related packages. You upload one, then discover an issue with another. Or perhaps the packages are ready, but you still want someone to review them before consumers can access them.

Until now, the publishing workflow didn't provide this particular staging process directly on NuGet.org.

Staged publishing introduces that extra checkpoint.

How it works

Rather than immediately making a package public, you can upload it to NuGet.org for staging.

The package goes through validation, but consumers cannot access it as a normal published package. You can then review the result and decide when to approve its promotion.

The general process looks like this:

- Prepare your NuGet package.
- Upload it using the staging workflow.
- Wait for NuGet.org to validate it.
- Review the package and its validation status.
- Approve its promotion when you're satisfied.
- Monitor the release as it becomes publicly available.

This is particularly useful when preparing coordinated releases involving multiple packages.

NuGet also supports staging groups, allowing related packages to be organized together.

There is one detail worth remembering: promoting a group is not an atomic operation. Individual packages can become publicly available at different times as they move through the distribution process.

So, if your application depends on several packages being released together, you still need to plan for that possibility.

Staged packages are not the same as unlisted packages

This distinction is important.

An unlisted package is still available if someone knows its exact package version. It simply doesn't appear in normal search results.

A staged package, on the other hand, is not available to consumers through the normal public package distribution process.

That makes staging more suitable when you want to prepare and review a release before anyone can depend on it.

What about automated publishing?

This is another area where the feature becomes interesting.

Many development teams already use CI/CD pipelines to build, test and publish packages. Staged publishing gives them an opportunity to separate uploading a package from approving its public release.

For example, a pipeline can upload a package using staging-only credentials. Those credentials are restricted to staging rather than normal public publishing.

An authorized maintainer can then review the package and approve its promotion through NuGet.org.

This doesn't replace testing or proper secret management. It adds another layer of control to the release process.

Trying it from the command line

The .NET 11 RC2 SDK supports basic staged package uploads through the command line.

A staging upload can look like this:

dotnet package stage push ./artifacts/Contoso.Library.1.2.0.nupkg --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json --api-key "$NUGET_API_KEY"

You can also specify a staging group:

dotnet package stage push ./artifacts/Contoso.Library.1.2.0.nupkg --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json --api-key "$NUGET_API_KEY" --group november-release

Replace the package path, group name and API key with the values for your own release.

One thing to keep in mind: uploading a package is not the same as publishing it. You still need to review the validation results and approve promotion before consumers can access it.

For the full explanation, see the official announcement:

Introducing staged publishing on NuGet.org

https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/nuget-staged-publishing/

What These Updates Tell Us

At first glance, AI-assisted cross-platform development and NuGet package staging don't seem to have much in common.

But both highlight something happening across software development: we're getting more ways to work, and we're being given more control over how software is built and delivered.

AI can help developers explore implementations that might previously have required more time or a larger team. New publishing workflows can help maintainers introduce better checks before releasing packages to the public.

Neither removes the need to understand what we're building.

You still need to know whether an architecture is appropriate, whether a performance improvement is meaningful, whether generated code is reliable and whether a package is ready for other developers to depend on.

Tools can make the work easier. Good engineering decisions are still our responsibility.

Something to Try This Week

If you're working with .NET MAUI, take a look at the Barista Notes experiment. You don't need to rebuild an entire application to learn something from it. Think about one screen in an application you've built and consider whether a shared interface or a platform-specific implementation makes more sense.

If you maintain NuGet packages, spend some time exploring staged publishing. Consider whether separating package uploads from public release approval could improve your current workflow.

Even if you don't use either feature immediately, understanding what they offer is useful.

Your Turn

I'm curious about how other .NET developers see this.

If you were starting a cross-platform mobile application today, would you use .NET MAUI for the entire application, build native interfaces while sharing the underlying C# logic, or combine both approaches?

And for those who publish NuGet packages, do you think staged publishing will change how you handle releases?

Share your thoughts. I'd be interested in hearing what you've tried and what works for your projects.

---

References

- AI is Changing the Cross-Platform Decision Matrix — .NET Blog, November 20, 2026.
  https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/ai-cross-platform-decision-matrix/

- Introducing staged publishing on NuGet.org — .NET Blog, November 17, 2026.
  https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/nuget-staged-publishing/
